data.title: Robert Müller: The region around the River Zala in the 8th–10th centuries
data.excerpt: Robert Müller's lecture follows the marshy lower Zala by Lake Balaton from the late Avar period to the Hungarian conquest. Translated for us by Kvetka M., it traces the Christian Keszthely culture, the biritual cemeteries west of the river and Pribina's centre at Mosaburg/Zalavár.
data.metaTitle: Robert Müller: the River Zala region, 8th–10th centuries
data.metaDescription: A translated lecture by Robert Müller on Avar and Slavic occupation around the River Zala by Lake Balaton and on Pribina's centre at Mosaburg/Zalavár.

children.text: With the help of our collaborator Kvetka M. we bring you a translation of another article on research into Slavic occupation and hillforts in the Lake Balaton region of Hungary.
Robert Müller: The region around the River Zala in the 8th–10th centuries

In this lecture I shall deal with the archaeological monuments of south-western Transdanubia, from the region around the River Zala, from the 8th to the 10th century. The Zala is the largest watercourse flowing into Lake Balaton, which it enters at its western end. In the last centuries of the first millennium the natural conditions were quite different from those of today. In the later part of the Migration Period there was a dry phase during which the level of Lake Balaton was considerably lower – this is attested by the 8th-century settlement at Fonyód-Békatelep, which lies about 2 m below the present-day level (Gyulai, 1987, 124). The western lake basin corresponded to the present-day area of the Little Balaton with open water, but the northern bay towards Hévíz had already been turned into peat bog by that time and had dried out so much that a road led across it from Keszthely westwards to the low hills near Zalavár. The ferry at the end of the peninsula at Fenékpuszta thus lost its importance. In the 8th century Keszthely became a new centre and the long-distance trade route ran through Balatonhídvég, where the Zala flowed into the lake.

At the end of the 8th century this area presented a peculiar and ethnically very varied picture, with the River Zala forming a kind of boundary. The surroundings of Keszthely had been continuously inhabited since Roman times. Within a radius of about 30 km here there are cemeteries of the so-called Keszthely culture, whose bearers belonged to the remnant of the Late Antique population, to which, after the Avars took control of Transdanubia (568), various groups of people from the Byzantine area were added, and Germanic people too were probably settled here (or migrated here) (Müller, 1992, 253-254, 278). This Christian population lived here relatively independently in a peripheral area of the Early Avar Khaganate. The ruling stratum lived in the fortification at Keszthely-Fenékpuszta (Sági, 1961, Barkóczi, 1968) and probably maintained regular contacts with the Balkans and northern Italy. Around 630 this leading stratum took the side that was later defeated during the internal struggles in the Avar Empire. Punishment did not pass it by: the victorious Avars captured the fortress, razed it to the ground, and the stratum that had ruled here until then disappeared. Those who survived were resettled in Keszthely (Kovrig, 1958, 68-72). The people of the Keszthely culture came under Avar military domination and the Avars began to settle this area too. Gyenesdiás (Müller, 1989), east of Keszthely, became the centre of military command. In the Middle and Late Avar periods, when the borders of the Avar Empire shifted to the west and south-west, this Christian population found itself in the interior of the empire and was isolated from the outside world. It could not keep pace with the changes of fashion in Christian Europe, and so its craftsmen merely went on copying older ornaments (jewellery), which gradually became larger and coarser. By the end of the 8th century basket-shaped earrings sometimes reached a diameter of as much as 8 cm, and pins (Stilusnadeln) were not infrequently longer than 30 cm. Disc brooches with Christian motifs disappeared, but bracelets with a snake's head at the end spread as something new. Such material has been found in at least 14 cemeteries, which is why the name Keszthely culture is justified (Kovrig, 1958, 1960, Müller, 1992). Most of these cemeteries were used jointly with the Avars, but within the cemetery these graves lay in a separate area. This means that they were able to preserve their ethnic identity for whole centuries, which can be explained by their Christian faith. Their burial rite is quite different from the Avar one; they adopted only a few types of jewellery (for example melon-seed-shaped beads, certain types of earring, wire bracelets). Alongside the shared cemeteries we also find purely Avar cemeteries, such as that at Gyenesdiás. The total size of the local community was not large, but towards the end of the 8th century the number of those buried here grew considerably.

And not only here! West of the River Zala the settlements developed quite differently. This area had remained practically unoccupied since Roman times. At the beginning of the 7th century cemeteries were then established here that are downright unusual for the Avar period within the Carpathian arc. These cemeteries are biritual and belong to the Pókaszepetk-Zalakomár group (Szőke, 1994, 14-20, Cs. Sós – Salamon, 1995). The cremated remains in the cremation graves were found both in urns and without urns; there were also cases of partial cremation of the dead, and biritual graves. The finds reveal that the dead were placed on the pyre clothed and with their jewellery (ornaments). Sometimes further offerings were placed in the graves after cremation. The inhumation graves are typically Early Avar with the usual grave goods; only some customs can be regarded as unusual: the belts often end in cast so-called Byzantine buckles and metal mounts are rare. Double graves of a man with a woman (“widow sacrifice”) occur frequently; sometimes as many as three people are buried in one grave. Forged (repoussé?) metal components also occur rarely on horse harness, and it is remarkable that with many horses a clay vessel was placed on the saddle. It is thought that these cemeteries for Avars and Slavs were established after the Avars marched against the Antes in 602 under the command of Apsich, and from that campaign brought here and settled the captured Du(d)lebs (Szőke, 1992, 139-143). Around 670–680 these cemeteries were abandoned and this population returned only after roughly a century. Most of the cemeteries were then used again and contained biritual graves.

We know almost no written sources about the Avars from the 8th century. The situation changes from 791, after Charlemagne's successful campaign against the Avars. We may assume that when in 796 Pippin organised a conference on the Danube, attended by the Patriarch of Aquileia and the Bishop of Salzburg, on the future conversion of the Avars, and when Christians living among the Avars together with their own priests were spoken of, this referred in part to the population of the Keszthely culture. The Slavs living between the rivers Zala and Mura can also be identified from 9th-century sources, in which place names in this area such as Tudleipin and Dudleipa are mentioned. The most important source for this area is the Conversio Bagoariorum et Carantanorum (hereafter CBC), written in Salzburg around 870, which deals mainly with events in the area around Zalavár.

The great changes in political and power relations after the collapse of the Avar Empire were reflected in the history of the local settlements only later. The cemeteries used previously continued in use at first. In the grave offerings, however, a change can already be seen. The graves are increasingly poor; in Avar male graves we find ever fewer decorated (repoussé) belts, and in the end decorated belts disappear completely. In female graves, too, simple wire earrings with a multiple S-shaped terminal or with a spiral pendant appear ever more frequently, and pieces imported from the west also appear. Only some warrior graves are richly furnished, above all one group of rich graves from the cemetery established at the end of the 8th century at Vörs-Papkert B (Költő-Szentpéteri, 1990, 69-78).

The cemeteries of the Keszthely culture were the first to be abandoned, before the end of the first third of the 9th century. This is certainly also connected with the fact that the local Christian population, thanks to its traditions, adapted to the new situation much more easily, and shortly after the missionaries from Salzburg began their work it gave up its distinctive costume and buried its dead in the western manner, mostly without grave goods, around the newly built churches. This makes them harder for archaeology to trace. How long the Avar cemeteries could have continued in use is disputed. Besides the view that they were used until the middle of the 9th century (Szőke, 1992b), we can also imagine that they were abandoned even before the settlement agglomeration at Zalavár came into being. A few poor cemeteries were founded only at the beginning of the 9th century by immigrant groups of people, as for example at Balatonszentgyörgy (Müller, 1994a, 66-67).
Great changes come about around 840 with the appearance and the activity of Pribina. As the CBC puts it:

blocks.text: Meanwhile … the king … granted Priwina in benefice a region in Lower Pannonia which lies on the River Zala. He then settled there, built himself a fortress in the marshy woods around the Zala, gathered people about him and became a great lord in that land.
blocks.author: Conversio Bagoariorum et Carantanorum

children.text: In fact we have no exact data today as to whether the marshy area on the lower course of the Zala, the individual islands and the shoreline strips were already occupied before 840. At the same time this means that the discovery of the cemeteries and settlements founded here plays an important role in the absolute dating of Central European finds of the 9th century. The regular excavations on the castle island of Zalavár, as well as the many necessary rescue excavations in the wider area connected with the Little Balaton project, have yielded a detailed picture of the settlement agglomeration at Zalavár (urbs paludarum). After 840 this area was densely occupied. The princely court on the castle island (Vársziget) at Zalavár was protected by a repeatedly renewed fortification of beams with a stone-and-timber construction. In the northern part of the island there was in addition a palisade wall, which evidently enclosed the residence of Pribina and Koceľ themselves. Inside this residence stood a three-aisled church with a semicircular apse and a large porch on the western side (Westwerk). The remains of the walls of a crypt with a circular ground plan also came to light. Beneath the floor fragments of gilded and of coloured window glass were found, which show a certain affinity with the window glass from Lorsch. The identification of this large church is disputed: it is described as the Church of the Virgin Mary (Cs. Sós, 1994, 87-90), but also as the Church of St Hadrian (Szőke, 1994, 47); both are mentioned in the CBC. In the southern part of the island there also stood a three-aisled church, which in recent centuries has completely collapsed. Its ground plan is known from a survey made in the 16th century, but the graves around the church show that it too was built in the 9th century (Cs. Sós, 1963, 42-68). The CBC mentions a third church as well, dedicated to St John the Baptist. In this case researchers agree that it is the likewise three-aisled church on the island of Récéskút. The assumption that two timber or stone-and-timber churches stood here before the stone churches has been refuted (Szőke, 1976, 76-84). To the south-west of the castle island a manorial court (curtis) was founded. A palisade enclosure with a square ground plan protected a timber church and probably also a half-timbered manor house (Müller, 1994). This manorial court may perhaps be identified with the residence of Wittimar, where at Christmas 864 Archbishop Adalwin dedicated a church to St Stephen the Martyr.

Around all the churches lay cemeteries in which the dead were buried according to Christian custom. This means that the great majority of graves were without grave goods. Only a few graves contained jewellery and ornaments, mostly of precious metals, and in male graves tools, weapons or spurs. Food offerings occur only occasionally. The best parallels for the jewellery found are known from Great Moravian cemeteries, but pieces originating in other regions also occur.

Service people were settled around the centre of Mosaburg. In the marshy terrain the islands and both banks of the river were linked by numerous timber causeways (“Knüppelwegen") (Csalog, 1960). Their cemeteries have an entirely different character. They are never situated around a church, and all the pagan customs continue to survive strongly here (Müller – Szőke, 1989, 84-96, Müller, 1992a, Szőke, 1992a). It seems that some cemeteries (Esztergályhorváti-Alsóbárándpuszta, Zalaszabar-Kisesztergály) were founded in pagan sacred groves, for graves are absent within large circles 10–15 m in diameter; in only one case was a cripple buried precisely in the centre of such a circle – towards the edges of the circles, by contrast, the number of graves becomes denser. Almost every grave contained an offering of food or drink. This is attested by poultry bones, eggs, more rarely bones of pig, cattle or sheep/goat, and also by pottery vessels, table pottery with a burnished surface and small wooden buckets. The jewellery is similar to that in the Christian cemeteries, but mostly only of bronze and only rarely of silver. Some communities also performed armed service (Garabonc-Ófalu I), which is attested by the weapons placed in graves. Weapons were also found in the cemetery at Keszthely-Fenékpuszta, where the fortification was renewed in the middle of the 9th century and a cemetery was laid out in front of its southern gate. Pagan customs are likewise evident in this cemetery (Cs. Sós, 1961), but they differ from those in the cemeteries around Zalavár (Bóna, 1968, 119). Further away still, about 20 km west of Mosaburg-Zalavár, in the cemetery of Alsórajk the dead were still being buried biritually in the second half of the 9th century (Szőke, 1994, 49). It appears that at Vörs the Late Avar population used its cemetery continuously until the arrival of the Hungarians, and here too the arrival (immigration) of a further ethnic group must be reckoned with (Költő-Lengyel-Pap-Szentpéteri, 1992).

As regards the 9th century we may state that above all most of the cemeteries established earlier – some of them as late as the end of the 8th century – continued in use. The cemeteries of the Keszthely culture were abandoned first, later also most of the purely Avar or Avar-Slavic biritual cemeteries. The restructuring of the settlement network may also have been connected with the construction of the new centre of power and administration at Mosaburg-Zalavár. On the basis of the large number of cemeteries we conclude that the area around the lower course of the River Zala was very densely occupied in the 9th century. Alongside the descendants of the region's original population we can trace, from written sources as well as from medieval geographical names, the arrival of various ethnic communities, such as South Slavs, West Slavs and Germanic people. The archaeological material does not make it possible to determine the ethnic affiliation of the groups and communities mentioned with absolute certainty, because the great majority of the finds were trade goods (Handelsware) corresponding to the general Central European fashion of the time, though admittedly with regional peculiarities as well. Far more results may be expected from anthropological-morphological and serological research. The osteological material processed so far shows that here on the River Zala we must reckon, besides the descendants of the original population of the immediate area, with groups that came from more distant parts of the Carpathian Basin, from Moravia, from the Frankish area, and also from Carinthia, with South Slavs (Timocanen und Abodriten), and that we must even reckon with Bulgars from the Danube (Éry, 1992, Szőke, 1994, 49-50).

We have seen that the collapse of the Avar Empire was reflected in the archaeological material above all indirectly. Even fewer changes could be observed after the great turning point at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries, when after 900, and later after the Battle of Bratislava in 907, the whole of Transdanubia came under Hungarian rule. The settlements of the 9th century continued to be inhabited and their cemeteries also remained in use. That the leading stratum of the Carolingian period had disappeared is attested only by indirect signs. At the manorial court on the island of Borjúállás, for example, the palisade wall was pulled down, so that nothing any longer prevented the cemetery from expanding spatially. In the cemeteries around the churches pagan phenomena also somehow increase.

According to tradition and to sources from the Árpád period, the area north and west of Lake Balaton fell to the third most important Hungarian tribe (Kál horka – one of Árpád's commanders), the Lád or Vérbulcsú tribe. Nevertheless, the Hungarians did not settle in this territory at first. Only in the cemetery at Vörs were graves found with finds typical of the conquerors of the land. The Late Carolingian population went on living in peace into the first half of the 10th century as well. We do not know when burial ceased in most of the cemeteries. One thing is certain: the characteristic ornaments of the common people which spread across the whole Carpathian Basin by about the middle of the 10th century, the so-called Bijelo Brdo culture, have not been found in the local cemeteries. Bijelo Brdo material is known only from the castle island (Zalavár); only there can continuity be reckoned with. But no traces of devastation can be observed at the abandoned settlements either. In the places abandoned by the original population the Hungarians do not appear at first. Only in the last third of the 10th century do the first finds left by the Hungarian common people appear, but these people did not settle in the marshy terrain on the islands or on the banks of the river, but on the higher ridges of sandy hillocks (Müller, 1991, 171-172, Tettamanti, 1971, 244).
